en: The *Dharmapada-gāthā on the Extinction of Phenomena* Spoken by the Buddha and Transmitted by the Bhikṣu Kātyāyana; consisting of one hundred and twenty chapters;
the translator’s name is lost, and it is now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra, having realized the Way and cultivated the Vinaya,
beheld those who were violent and impetuous; he opened the path of the Dharma with verses,
his heart constantly harboring sorrow and regret as he contemplated matters of compassionate grief.
Constantly exert yourself with diligence; look back with great trepidation.
The True Dharma is on the verge of extinction; when the human lifespan is but a hundred years, the radiance of the True Dharma will soon vanish from the world.
When the True Dharma has utterly perished, the assembly of bhikṣus will be deluded;
they shall abandon the various sūtras and dharmas taught by the Awakened Sage,
instead accepting miscellaneous literary compositions and discarding what the Buddha himself spoke.
Seeing them instructed by shallow sutras, their minds are filled with delight;
they constantly engage in disputes, contravening the teachings and turning their backs on the scriptures,
spreading slander one after another, and each showing mutual contempt.
Foolish and difficult to transform through instruction, lacking wisdom like a withered stump,
you have no discerning knowledge; having failed to study the Buddha’s True Dharma,
you abandon the principles and meanings of the sutras, seeking only each other's faults.
What I have heard and transmitted from my own person is peerless and without companion;
holding the center, one fixes it below, and raising what is below, one fixes it in the center, no longer perceiving any sequence.
What is thus explained is noble and inexhaustible.
When the realization of the locus is erroneous, they conversely claim there is neither beginning nor end;
both hearing and receiving are superficial and empty, while their discourse lacks pure conversation.
These people harbor evil intentions and slander their preceptors.
Seeing the Honored One, the Teacher, they are arrogant and do not show reverence;
such as these engage in mutual dispute. Their minds are filled with deep sorrow and poison;
attached to the world and longing for wealth and nobility, they fall into bondage without realizing it.
I have realized the most sublime truth, yet you truly know nothing;
your discourse is utterly erroneous, while my words accord with the scriptural principles.
As we each dispute and contend, we give rise to hearts of malice.
Greedy for gain and offerings, they sink and float along with worldly customs;
Habituated to the pleasures of dwelling in houses, they cannot extricate themselves.
Following others, they engage in conversation out of greed, Speaking only of mundane affairs.
At that time, the bhikṣus abandoned the spaces between trees and secluded dwellings to reside in villages;
they established monasteries between two [communities] and took delight in the clamor of the crowd, having no longing for quietude.
They deceive and encroach upon one another in turn to provide for their own wives and children;
yet there may be times when a bhikṣu arrives as a guest from a distant land,
and the abbot of the monastery first settles himself comfortably before allowing the guest to dwell in peace.
They are envious of where he dwells; they resent his virtue and reputation, and likewise resent his noble lineage.
Furthermore, when they hear of a bhikṣu from a distant land who has come to see the Dharma, their countenances lose their harmony and serenity.
When one attains the relinquishment of these things, the mind finds true joy.
Yet, those who are greedily attached to offerings give rise to poisonous malice, jealousy, arrogance, and pride;
because of this, they fall into resentment and ruin.
Constantly harboring thoughts of anger and malice, Proud and conceited,
never satisfied with what they seek; Following their own whims,
they indulge in defiled and poisonous matters that ought not to be practiced, And have no desire to recite or receive the sutras.
All day long they laugh, sing, and dance; at nightfall, they sleep until dawn without waking.
These people gather together, their speech never touching upon principles of governance, but speaking only of the officials as thieves—this is the conduct of the prevailing customs.
Suppose there were one who trains, envied and honored by the multitude,
seeking to go forth from the household life; suppose there were one who trains,
claiming to study the Dharma of a bhikṣu, and revered by those in white robes.
Devoted to trivial matters, he gained fame thereby;
his conduct did not accord with the teachings,
as he pursued gain and honor from his youth, gathering many disciples around him.
With minds harboring strife and turmoil, they cannot fathom what they have studied;
as śramaṇas for two or three years, they gather many followers,
yet none are able to be prudent regarding the precepts, falling instead into false views.
Some preach annihilationism; others teach that there is a person who abides in such training.
They fall into the ways of base men;
their disciples, with hair and beards shorn, are for the most part vulgar and loathsome, surrounded by youths.
At times there is severe drought, and at other times there are great floods;
sparrows, mice, and locusts—calamities arrive all at once.
The five grains are utterly exhausted, and the common people all suffer from famine.
Driven to the brink by the struggle for daily sustenance, he left the household life seeking peace;
he then became a śramaṇa, yet was undisciplined and transgressed the rules,
failing to understand the prohibitions, so that the assembly had no one to protect them.
Being negligent and devoid of shame, they are unable to cultivate prudent conduct nor do they delight in the Dharma assemblies;
they are anxiously preoccupied with the accumulation of wealth and regard what is unrighteous as righteous,
such that their speech contradicts the Way and its principles.
When accusing others of offenses, they reverse the gravity of the matter; they disrupt the scriptures and oppose the precepts of the sages.
Assemblies continue until midnight, and disputes grow ever more extensive;
only then do they preach the sutras, doing so in a cursory and incomplete manner.
Rarely will they explain the prohibitions and precepts;
being full of strife and contention, they lose the meaning and principle in every instance.
Thus, as the True Dharma comes to its end, having just engaged in quarreling, they subsequently bind themselves in enmity.
The various Māras and their retinues, taking advantage of this opportunity,
along with devas, nāgas, and spirits, have come desiring to hear the teachings of the sūtra;
they yearn and wait longingly to hear the precepts, yet instead they hear only further disputes and litigation.
The devas and humans harbor resentment; they cannot endure the bhikṣu’s conduct as he comes and goes.
They say together: "The Buddha-dharma is about to perish completely;
we have abandoned our celestial pleasures, and thus we have come desiring to receive the Dharma."
They shall not hear the True Dharma; it is better for them to abandon it.
Those who revere spirits and deities will find no joy in the Buddha-Dharma, nor will they think of the bhikṣus, and they will no longer practice protection.
At that time, malevolent spirits and ghosts, acting with fierce violence and inflicting poison and harm,
will seize the vital essence of the bhikṣus, leaving them with no life remaining;
the bhikṣus will suffer many illnesses, becoming emaciated, weak, and devoid of strength.
They lose their senses and their complexions change; through diligent toil they encounter manifold calamities.
They revile and envy one another in turn, and when illness strikes, they do not look after each other.
Some even reach death, perishing prematurely without protection.
Clinging greedily to wealth and treasures, with no moderation in food or clothing,
they understand the ways of worldly custom and sustain themselves through wrongful occupations.
They engage in trade and commerce for profit, seeking interest on their capital as they move in and out of business.
Their aspirations still lie in mundane affairs; they strive tirelessly yet find no end to their involvement in trivial matters.
Seeking profit and desiring to save their own lives, they abandon the practice that leads to transcendence;
thus, they entangle themselves in petty concerns.
Their robes are not properly arranged, and they are unpracticed in the observance of ritual decorum;
unable to act in accordance with the Way, they are like wild horses or monkeys.
Yet, seeing a worthy bhikṣu from afar, they know to practice restraint and contentment when seeking alms.
From afar they reviled him, saying:
"He does not comply with the prohibitions like the bhikṣus of today; he remains serene and free from fault.
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent while committing many evils.
Those who steal and act with guile without shame or remorse, who are indolent and harbor poisonous intent—
such as these shall, in future ages, instead be honored and served by virtuous and noble bhikṣus who are fully endowed with integrity and a sense of shame.
When that Dharma has perished, one no longer finds anyone to rely upon;
like a lion king dwelling amidst the forest trees,
jackals, wolves, dogs, and foxes dare not eat its flesh.
When life has passed and worms emerge from the body, they devour their own flesh;
day and night they feed together, destroying the physical form.
This is what occurs after the Great Sage, the Man of Supreme Wisdom, has entered *nirvāṇa* and passed away.
The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind cannot destroy the Buddha-dharma, that rare and wondrous treasure of the world;
it does not vanish through negligence or falsehood.
While common gold may appear in the world, the purple-gold [of the Dharma] remains unmanifested.
While the True Dharma remains in the world, it never perishes of its own accord;
yet because of the existence of the Semblance Dharma, the True Dharma is extinguished.
It is like a ship upon the sea: through the burden of greed, it sinks.
The Buddha-dharma is likewise thus: through gain and offerings, it will utterly perish.
Turning their backs on the sūtras and the sacred scriptures, they take this as the true Dharma;
they act contrary to the Dharma and violate the Vinaya, establishing doctrines that are not in accordance with the Dharma.
Those of various heterodox views and false doctrines, and the scholars possessing the five supernatural powers,
cannot destroy the meaning of the Dharma; nor can they obstruct the acts of giving undertaken by those who follow Śākyamuni,
for it is because of the Buddha that they have become śramaṇas.
When they destroy the True Dharma, causing the Dharma to reach its total extinction;
when those inferior men, having shaved their hair and donned the *kāṣāya*,
all bring about the ruin of the True Dharma, and cause the scriptures to vanish and no longer appear.
Unwilling to comply with the prohibitions and teachings, they exert their strength to preserve their own legalistic agendas;
indulging their hearts in whatever they please, they are like donkeys covered in dust.
At that time, those students receive and grasp [these views], falsely maintaining them as authoritative.
Having altered those various vouchers, they cause the letters entrusted to them to be misplaced;
thus, they stand in fear of the county officials, resentful bandits, and creditors,
trembling with mutual malice and hardship, so terrified that their hair stands on end.
Plowing fields, raising crops, and managing livelihoods; encountering various officials and soldiers;
daily practicing impure desires; being tormented by the afflictions seen by the multitude—there will be three evil kings, with the Great Qin at their head.
Parthia shall be in the rear, An-hsi (Parthia) shall be in the center;
Because of this, the True Dharma will be abandoned and lost.
The Yi (Yuezhi) kings, most cruel and evil, shall dwell in the north.
Raising armies to invade evil nations and harming the myriad people;
Slighting and disparaging the śramaṇas and committing many manifold evils;
Destroying Buddha-stūpas and temples, and ruining the monasteries where the learned dwell.
At that time, the world’s provinces and states shall all become ruins;
these people, filled with fear, sorrow, and anguish,
will abandon the lands of the north and flee toward the Middle Kingdom.
Sickly and emaciated, with sight failing, Wasted by consumption and lacking strength,
unable to leave the north, At that time, when he is to be harmed,
The young bhikṣu who does not strive in the life of a śramaṇa.
He immediately cast off his garments, terrified and seeking to preserve himself;
thus the ruler of the Middle Kingdom came to punish the King of the Barbarians.
Having already executed the King of the Barbarians, he returned to reside in Kaṇi.
There was a venerable bhikṣu there, Whose name was Śiśa;
he was widely learned and there was nothing he did not master. He was able to delight all the kings;
when the kings heard Śiśa’s words, Their hearts were filled with joy and exultation.
Wishing to invite the assembly of monks, he prepared a great act of giving.
He dispatched messengers to the ten directions to proclaim his command throughout all lands:
"All people, come here; now I shall perform a great act of giving."
All the monks gathered together, numbering in the hundreds of thousands;
having encountered this calamity, they were all haggard and withered. They longed to see the Great Giver.
Once the bhikṣus had assembled, the hundreds of thousands were fully prepared.
They turn to one another in search [of the truth],
each inquiring after the whereabouts of those who are kind and benevolent; they follow wherever their preceptors go,
and now take as their teachers those who were once their śrāmaṇeras.
Some were wounded, some died, and others were driven away;
when the bhikṣus saw one another, they wept, unable to restrain themselves.
At that time, those gathered there numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
Bearing resentment, they lost their composure; though they delighted in seeing great acts of giving,
they gathered from all four directions on the fifteenth day for an assembly to recite the Buddha’s scriptures and precepts,
only to fall into mutual anger and strife immediately thereafter.
Since these individuals are thus filled with resentment and indignation, and continue to act in mutual discord, the Venerable Bhikṣu has issued this instruction: "The various bhikṣus remain silent;
I shall now speak to you all and show you the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
Listen to what I say: do not allow your speech to be confused.
This Jambudvīpa is a gathering of śramaṇas and disciples of the Buddha;
you should all be in harmony together, for it is not right to harbor long-standing resentment.
There was a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
who desired to study the meaning of the Path; they gathered for the fifteenth-day assembly,
though the great assembly of bhikṣus numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
I have studied and attained clear understanding; you all cannot know it.
If there be a bhikṣu who, through study, has attained realization, let him then explain its beginning and end; I have studied and know its sūtra.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose learning was universal and who was renowned for his virtue,
named Sūrata; having thus uttered this lion’s roar,
he immediately rose from his seat and stood with palms joined.
I bow my head at the feet of the Elder; I shall now let out a lion’s roar.
I harbor no doubts, and my mind is free from hesitation.
Regarding the sūtras and precepts I have studied, I have now attained mastery over them.
I am free from all difficulties, and my mind neither advances nor retreats.
That which I have previously studied, the Dharma and Vinaya, I know without doubt;
I am thoroughly versed in the scriptures and clearly enlightened in the meaning of the Path.
"My learning is such as this; you worthy ones should uphold it.
You have not mastered the various scriptures, nor do you understand the Vinaya and Dharma.
Why, then, in the presence of the Venerable One, do you so frequently praise yourself?"
The Venerable Teacher had a wicked disciple, By nature fierce and harboring malice;
his name was Asita. He then proceeded to harm Sūrata, at which time there was a great spirit Who had faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma.
Holding a vajra in his hand, he then struck and killed Asitaṃgu;
at that time in the world, the earth shook six times in all directions,
and non-human beings spontaneously beat the divine drums.
At that time, from the four directions, there shall arise four great mists and likewise four great fires; from above and from the four quarters,
they shall descend upon your world, and at that time, the world will become shrouded in darkness.
From this point on, there shall be no returning; sentient beings have sunk into ignorance, and the masses are beyond counting.
Today, in this final age of decline, they harbor grief and anguish;
yet the Buddha’s True Dharma has not yet come to an end.
Having once seen Buddhas and spirits, they believed with joy in the meaning of the Path;
now casting their bodies prostrate upon the ground, they wail and collapse, unable to support themselves.
When the bhikṣus encounter such calamity, it is like a person losing both parents.
Today is the final age; the Buddha’s True Dharma shall be extinguished.
From this day forward, there will no longer be the preaching of the sūtras, the Vinaya, or the prohibitive precepts. From whom, then, shall we hear and listen?
The celestial trees and spirits, the deities dwelling in the wilderness,
their hearts moved by compassion, were filled with grief and anxiety; they could not find peace, turning this way and that,
for the lamp of the Dharma has already set and the authentic scriptures have been destroyed.
Now this world is utterly collapsed; The Dharma drum no longer sounds.
All the Māras rejoice, Assembling to offer their congratulations.
Raising their hands, they praise, saying: "Now is the final age of the Buddha."
In future ages to come, there shall be such calamities;
therefore, one should apply even greater diligence and strive with all one's might for deliverance.
It is like a merchant who, having lost his opportunity, harbors distress in his heart.
Therefore, you should increase your devotion and attachment; do not let yourself regret it later.

When you hear that the Way and Dharma are flourishing, that the scriptures are widely disseminated, and that those who preach the Dharma constantly remain, cultivate the Buddha's teachings with a diligent mind.
Today, the fourfold assembly Respect one another in turn;
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma still endures, They exert themselves with diligence day and night.
Their bodies are naturally healthy and strong, Having not yet encountered old age, sickness, or death.
For this reason, you should be diligent; be mindful of the great peril that lies ahead.

When times are peaceful in all lands, free from manifold calamities and hardships, when harvests are bountiful and alms are easily obtained, one should reverently practice the prohibitions of the Buddha’s teachings.
The śramaṇa Khaṇḍarāṣṭra, having heard this Dharma teaching and precept,
bowed his head in prostration before him; the elder Kātyāyana, for his part,
felt his body tremble, his hair stood on end, and his heart grew cold with fear.
Having lost their resolve and not knowing the Dharma, they no longer recognize the directions.
Now that I have heard these words, my heart is filled with great fear;
seeing this in future lives, how could my heart not shatter?
After the Venerable Kaccāyana had expressed this sorrow, he preached the True Dharma for his disciples.
For three hundred years, many attained liberation; for another three hundred years, they heard the teachings on morality and concentration.
For three hundred years he repaired Buddhist temples; entering the Green Garden for a thousand years, he spoke of the monk’s joy and lack of joy.
Practicing solitude, dwelling upon his mat, he moved without fixed direction; thus he should subdue all cravings and desires.
The Buddha commissioned the bhikṣu Kātyāyana to preach the Dharma through one hundred and twenty stanzas on the verse of the exhaustion of existence.
